cross_run_instability_finding.summary: Pair #1 (souls -> World) and pair #3 (souls -> Sun) were also classified in round 1 (data/fascicle34_worked_example_ground_truth.json), by a separately-run, independently-blind agent instance, using the same taxonomy definitions. Round 1 called 'souls -> World' an amplifier (matching this run) but called 'souls -> Sun' an amplifier too -- this run calls the same pair 'Uncategorized.' Multiple other pairs classified in both round 3 and this final run also received different labels across runs (e.g. 'exorbitant -> importunate': 'Substitutive (undefined)' in round 3, 'Amplifiers' here).
cross_run_instability_finding.implication: This is a real limitation worth stating plainly, not smoothing over: LLM-based classification against a qualitatively-defined taxonomy is not perfectly stable run to run, even applying the identical category definitions to the identical pair. The 'Substitutive (undefined)' rate specifically dropped from 32-56% across rounds 1-3 (56 pairs, partial dataset) to 14% in this final run (84 pairs, complete dataset) -- likely because this run's prompt explicitly offered 'uncategorized' as a standing option, which absorbed cases that earlier runs, without that option made equally salient, defaulted to 'Substitutive.' The honest conclusion is not 'the taxonomy gap was overstated' or 'the taxonomy gap is confirmed at 14%' -- it's that the true rate is sensitive to how the classification task itself is specified, and any single number from any single run should be reported as exactly that: one run's result, not a stable population parameter.
